extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent litigators, IP counsel and clients considering Inter Partes Review (IPR)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, procedural requirements, and practical considerations for filing and evaluating petitions for Inter Partes Review (IPR) at the USPTO Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB). Includes institution threshold, petition contents, allowable grounds, fees, timing, estoppel, and differences from re-examination/court proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution threshold (reasonable likelihood)
rubrics_metrics.description: The board may only institute an IPR if the petitioner, in its request, shows a reasonable likelihood that the patent is invalid. (cites 35 U.S.C. § 314).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners must meet the statutory standard of showing a reasonable likelihood of invalidity for at least one claim to trigger institution. This is the high bar the board uses to decide whether to grant review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition content requirement (claim-by-claim invalidity and prior art grounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: In its request, the petitioner must explain why each claim is invalid and show what previous publication or combination of publications render the claim invalid. Each set of invalidating art is a 'ground' of invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitions should identify the specific claim(s), articulate why each is invalid, and cite the prior art references or combinations relied on. Petitioners may assert multiple grounds for each claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of allowable grounds (anticipation and obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical grounds asserted include anticipation and obviousness over prior art. Each anticipatory reference or combination of art for obviousness is considered one asserted ground of invalidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation requires a single reference that teaches all elements of a claim; obviousness typically relies on combinations of references. The article observes the board finds obviousness challenges more persuasive than anticipation challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple grounds per claim allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: A petitioner may file multiple grounds for each claim, if it wishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategically, multiple grounds can increase chances of institution but increase complexity and cost; each ground is separately counted in analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing fee and refund policy
rubrics_metrics.description: To file a request for IPR, a petitioner must pay $23,000. If the board declines to initiate the proceeding, it will refund $14,000 of that amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IPR petitions are significantly more expensive than prior USPTO proceedings. The high cost may discourage weaker filings and influences client cost-benefit decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory timing for final determination
rubrics_metrics.description: The board is required by law to complete its determination within a year of instituting an IPR, or 18 months in extreme circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This short statutory timetable is an advantage over district-court litigation and is a key scheduling consideration when advising clients on pursuing IPR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of review (validity-only limitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The board focuses only on validity; unlike district-court trials, it does not decide infringement, damages, willfulness, enforceability, or counterclaims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because IPRs address only validity, they can be faster and less expensive but will not resolve infringement or damages issues; this limited scope is both a benefit and a limitation depending on client goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTAB expertise and internal technical resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The board, as part of the USPTO, has special expertise with patents and can draw on internal technical resources to make a more accurate determination than a judge or jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The technical and patent-focused composition of the board can favor technically complex analyses and may influence strategy when deciding forum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel consequences of PTAB decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the board finds the patent valid, the defendant is estopped from raising the same arguments that it raised or could have raised before the board. Once the board has made a determination, the trial court will not have to revisit that decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instituting an IPR and then losing can limit defenses in subsequent district-court litigation; petitioners must weigh estoppel risks when deciding what arguments and grounds to include.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences from old inter partes re-examination
rubrics_metrics.description: IPRs are determined by the board without involvement of patent examiners, are appealable directly to the Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, allow discovery between the parties, and involve an actual hearing before a three-judge panel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These procedural differences make IPRs more trial-like than re-examinations and affect evidentiary strategy, discovery planning, and appeal options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dismissals and voluntary terminations excluded from grant/deny statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: The board may dismiss, without decision, a request that does not meet the requirements of the IPR rules. Parties may voluntarily terminate a pending request. These do not count as either grants or denials in the published statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting institution/denial statistics, exclude dismissals and voluntary terminations to avoid misleading conclusions about institutional rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting methodology for statistical analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Each anticipatory reference or combination of art for obviousness is considered one asserted ground. Only when board decisions were unclear as to the number of grounds asserted does analysis use numbers from the original petitions instead of board decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about whether statistics are aggregated by petition, by claim, or by asserted ground; use original petitions to resolve ambiguities in board opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation caveat: institution ≠ final invalidation
rubrics_metrics.description: The board’s grant of the petition to review does not reflect the likelihood that the board will actually invalidate one or more claims of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clients should not equate institution rates with ultimate success rates; institution indicates a threshold showing of likely invalidity, not a final finding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observed early-stage trend: high grant rates and plausible explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: In the first nine months the board was granting review of the vast majority of petitions. Possible explanations include abnormally high quality of early petitions and the high cost/time to prepare petitions discouraging less-meritorious filers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use caution extrapolating early statistics into long-term expectations; consider market/practitioner behavior and cost-driven selection effects when advising clients.
